proposals.track: Software Architecture, Scalable Developer Tooling & Real-World AI
proposals.talk_title: Beyond the Cloud Token Tax: Re-Architecting Developer Tooling with Local-Silicon AST Context Slicing
proposals.subtitle: How Deterministic In-Process AST Parsing Slashes LLM Costs by 83.6% with Sub-1.4ms Latency
proposals.prerequisites: Familiarity with transformer-based LLMs, Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), and enterprise CI/CD workflows.
proposals.abstract_short: First-generation AI coding tools proxy raw files over external clouds, causing attention entropy dilution and massive monthly token bills. This session introduces deterministic local AST context slicing—using AVX-512 vector-accelerated Tree-sitter parsers to split code into Control and Execution planes, reducing token payloads by 83.6% in under 1.4ms with zero network egress.
proposals.abstract_full:
The rapid enterprise adoption of generative AI coding assistants has introduced an acute architectural tension between developer productivity and cybersecurity integrity. Commercial tools operate predominantly as cloud-proxied context ingestors, serializing active buffers and dispatching them over WAN proxies. In practice, transmitting raw source files introduces severe intellectual property exfiltration hazards while diluting LLM attention heads over boilerplate execution logic.

In this talk, we deconstruct the architecture of deterministic local-silicon Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) context slicing. Using in-process AVX-512 SIMD vector-accelerated Tree-sitter parsers, source code is decomposed into a Dual-Plane Context Topology: isolating public interface contracts (Control Plane) from redundant internal function bodies (Execution Plane). We demonstrate how this architecture achieves an 83.6% reduction in LLM token payloads in under 1.4 milliseconds of local CPU time with zero outbound network egress, amortizing capital investments within 18 calendar days across 1,000-developer organizations.
key_takeaways: Mathematical formulation of the Cloud Token Tax and attention entropy dispersion (H_attn ≈ log2 N).
Engineering implementation of Dual-Plane Context Topology (Control Plane vs Execution Plane).
SIMD vector acceleration of Tree-sitter grammars achieving 2.4 GB/s throughput in safe runtimes.
Empirical enterprise TCO models proving sub-21-day capital payback periods.

timed_outline.topics: The $142k/yr token bleed per 100 devs, attention dilution, unmonitored WAN proxies
Graph pruning algorithms, public interfaces vs private bodies, token reduction equations
Zero-copy grammar traversals, 142 MB RSS memory footprints, sub-1.4ms parse times
Real-time execution of omnikernel-bench on 50,000 LoC codebase
Payback metrics, $29 lifetime licensing vs SaaS bloat, open architectural Q&A

proposals.speaker_bio: OmniKernel Labs DevRel & Systems Advocacy Guild represents senior systems researchers, compiler engineers, and distributed systems architects specializing in deterministic local-first developer tooling, AST parsing, and zero-trust cryptographic enclaves.

proposals.talk_title: Attention Entropy Dispersion & Shannon Invariants: The Information Theory of Local Code Engines
proposals.subtitle: Unifying Transformer Self-Attention Mechanics with In-Register Shannon Entropy Bounds
proposals.prerequisites: Working knowledge of transformer self-attention, Shannon information theory, and basic SIMD vector instruction sets.
proposals.abstract_short: Modern AI coding tools treat code as unstructured natural language tokens, degrading attention mechanisms and leaking secrets. This talk formalizes the mathematics of Attention Entropy Dispersion in transformers and presents an AVX-512 SIMD kernel that computes real-time Shannon entropy (H >= 4.50 bits/char) to intercept secret keys in under 0.8ms without false positives on hexadecimal UUIDs.
proposals.abstract_full:
Modern generative AI coding tools treat source code as unstructured natural language tokens, ignoring the rigorous algebraic and semantic guarantees provided by compiler Abstract Syntax Trees. This mismatch leads to two catastrophic failures: attention entropy dispersion within transformer self-attention layers, and accidental secret credential leaks by autonomous agent loops.

This session presents a unified information-theoretic framework for developer tooling. First, we formalize Attention Entropy Dispersion: as context length N grows through naive file ingestion, the self-attention entropy scales logarithmically, diluting attention mass away from critical type signatures. We prove that AST context slicing restores attention concentration by projecting code onto its minimal interface manifold. Second, we explore real-time Shannon entropy analysis implemented within CPU SIMD registers, proving why hexadecimal UUIDs (bounded at H <= 4.00) never trigger false positives, while cryptographic private keys (H >= 4.50) are caught in under 0.8ms.
key_takeaways: Mathematical derivation of attention entropy dispersion in Transformer self-attention layers.
Shannon entropy boundaries for finite alphabets: Sigma_16 (UUIDs) vs Sigma_64 (Base64 keys).
Vectorized AVX-512 implementation of sliding-window entropy histograms executing in sub-0.8ms.
Enforcing POSIX-level invariant gates against autonomous agent test suite deletions.

timed_outline.section_title: The Information Theory of Code Synthesis
timed_outline.topics: Token representations vs compiler ASTs, entropy loss in unstructured ingestion
Logarithmic scaling of attention entropy, self-attention heatmap dilution proofs
The H >= 4.50 bits/char threshold, SIMD histogramming, eliminating UUID false alarms

timed_outline.section_title: Agentic Adversarial Loss Functions & Pre-Commit Traps
timed_outline.topics: Preventing autonomous agents from deleting failing tests via POSIX Exit Code 2
Open problems in AST-constrained generation

proposals.track: High-Assurance Systems, Sovereign Infrastructure & SCIF Security
proposals.talk_title: Deterministic Zero-Egress Runtimes: Enforcing SCIF-Grade Airgaps with In-Kernel eBPF and TPM 2.0 PCR Attestation
proposals.subtitle: Building Sovereign Developer Environments for Defense SCIFs, Banking Enclaves, and ITAR Facilities
proposals.prerequisites: Understanding of Linux networking, eBPF tracepoints, TPM 2.0 primitives, and physical air-gap concepts.
proposals.abstract_short: Cloud-based developer assistants are categorically barred from classified defense SCIFs and sovereign banking enclaves due to WAN egress risks. This talk outlines a zero-egress developer runtime combining in-kernel eBPF socket monitoring (sys_enter_connect), TPM 2.0 PCR hardware quote attestation, and NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 post-quantum key encapsulation to guarantee 0.00 KB network transmission.
proposals.abstract_full:
For defense primes, classified government facilities, and sovereign financial institutions operating within Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities (SCIFs), commercial cloud-proxied AI coding assistants are fundamentally non-compliant. These environments strictly prohibit outbound TCP sockets over WAN, unmonitored telemetric pings, or cloud license phone-home handshakes.

This talk presents an end-to-end systems architecture for a 100% air-gapped, zero-telemetry autonomous engineering runtime. We walk through: 1) Writing and attaching in-kernel eBPF probes to intercept sys_enter_connect and sock_ops syscalls, mathematically halting any non-loopback connection with EPERM; 2) Binding runtime licensing, AST indexing caches, and cryptographic keys to TPM 2.0 Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs 0-7, 10, 14) via signed hardware quotes; 3) Implementing NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM-768) lattice-based key encapsulation to counter nation-state 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' (HNDL) attacks. We conclude with a live demonstration of continuous 72-hour zero-egress verification.
key_takeaways: How to author and load eBPF socket-blocking probes to mathematically enforce zero WAN egress.
Implementing hardware-backed TPM 2.0 PCR quote extraction and offline signature validation.
Post-quantum cryptography deployment strategies using NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA).
Turnkey SCIF installation runbooks using optical data diodes and reproducible SLSA Level 3 builds.

timed_outline.section_title: The Threat Model of Cloud Proxies in SCIFs
timed_outline.topics: ICD 705 / CMMC 2.0 compliance, HNDL threat vector, why SaaS tools fail security audits

timed_outline.section_title: Linux eBPF Kernel Socket Monitoring & Enforcement
timed_outline.topics: Attaching to sys_enter_connect, packet drop verification, ring buffer telemetry

timed_outline.section_title: Hardware Root of Trust: TPM 2.0 PCR Quotes & Ed25519
timed_outline.topics: PCR register measurements, composite digests, offline cryptographic licensing
ML-KEM-768 M-LWE math, hybrid X25519 exchange, NSA CNSA 2.0 transition
72-hour packet capture proof, zero egress verification, open discussion

proposals.talk_title: High-Throughput SIMD Vectorization of Tree-sitter Grammars in Safe Rust: Achieving Sub-1.4ms AST Slicing at 2.4 GB/s
proposals.subtitle: Micro-architectural Tuning, Arena Allocations, and Zero-Copy FFI in Systems Rust
proposals.prerequisites: Proficiency in Rust, understanding of memory layouts, allocators, and basic SIMD vector instruction sets.
proposals.abstract_short: When parsing million-line enterprise repositories, naive syntax analysis bottlenecks on cache misses and allocation thrashing. This session details how we achieved 2.4 GB/s parsing throughput and sub-1.4ms AST context slicing in pure, safe Rust using AVX-512/NEON SIMD intrinsics, bumpalo arena allocators, and zero-copy Tree-sitter FFI wrappers.
proposals.abstract_full:
Tree-sitter is the industry standard for incremental syntax parsing, but when applied across enterprise monorepos comprising millions of lines of code, naive linear grammar traversal quickly bottlenecks on CPU cache misses, pointer indirection, and branch mispredictions. When building real-time developer tooling, syntax analysis must execute well under the 16-millisecond frame budget—ideally under 2 milliseconds—to prevent editor stutter.

This talk explores how we achieved 2.4 GB/s parsing throughput and sub-1.4 millisecond AST context slicing in pure, safe Rust. We dive deep into the micro-architectural optimizations that make this possible: 1) Vectorizing lexical token scans using AVX-512 and NEON SIMD intrinsics via std::arch; 2) Utilizing arena allocators (bumpalo) to eliminate heap allocation thrashing during AST graph traversal; 3) Zero-copy deserialization of concrete syntax trees into compact Control-Plane symbol representations; 4) Maintaining 100% safe Rust at the consumer boundary while interfacing with C Tree-sitter libraries. We inspect assembly output, examine perf stat metrics, and review cache miss reductions.
key_takeaways: Vectorizing text lexing and token classification using portable and target-specific SIMD intrinsics.
Micro-optimizations with bump allocation (bumpalo) and memory layout alignment to eliminate allocator overhead.
Benchmarking and profiling Rust binaries using perf stat, cargo-flamegraph, and LLVM assembly inspect tools.
Authoring zero-overhead, memory-safe FFI wrappers around C libraries.

timed_outline.topics: Why developer tooling cannot tolerate garbage collection or slow tree traversals

timed_outline.section_title: SIMD Vectorization of Lexical Scanners in Rust
timed_outline.topics: AVX-512 and NEON intrinsics, 64-byte chunks, assembly inspection
Eliminating heap fragmentation with bumpalo, cache-friendly flat tree representations

timed_outline.section_title: Safe FFI Integration with Tree-sitter C Run-Times
timed_outline.topics: Zero-copy pointer lifetimes, wrapping raw nodes in ergonomic safe Rust structs
Live execution of cargo flamegraph, analyzing L1/L2 cache hit improvements

proposals.talk_title: Building a Sub-110ms Duplex Voice Coding Engine with Go gRPC, WebRTC, and ONNX Silero VAD
proposals.subtitle: High-Concurrency Audio Pipelines, Zero-Allocation Buffer Slicing, and Verbal Barge-In
proposals.prerequisites: Working knowledge of Go concurrency (goroutines, channels, sync.Pool), WebRTC fundamentals, and gRPC streaming.
proposals.abstract_short: Traditional voice coding tools have 600ms–1500ms latencies, breaking developer flow. This talk reveals how to build a real-time duplex voice coding engine in Go with sub-110ms roundtrip response, local ONNX Silero VAD inference on CPU, WebRTC streaming, and instant verbal barge-in using sync.Pool zero-allocation techniques.
proposals.abstract_full:
Building voice-controlled developer tooling has traditionally been crippled by high network latencies and clumsy turn-taking protocols. When a developer has to pause for 800 milliseconds after speaking to hear an assistant's response, the cognitive flow state is broken. True conversational voice coding requires a duplex architecture capable of sub-110 millisecond roundtrip latency with support for seamless verbal barge-in.

This talk details how we engineered a sub-110ms duplex voice engine in Go. We walk through the architecture of a high-concurrency pipeline connecting: 1) Low-latency WebRTC audio streaming with local Acoustic Echo Cancellation (AEC3); 2) Local CPU inference of ONNX Silero Voice Activity Detection (VAD), processing 30ms audio chunks in under 8ms with zero cloud roundtrips; 3) A bi-directional gRPC streaming control plane orchestrating AST transformations and semantic code navigation; 4) Low-latency verbal barge-in ('CROW' protocol), allowing a developer to verbally interrupt an agent's code generation within 38 milliseconds. We share techniques for zero-allocation byte slicing with sync.Pool and managing Go runtime GC pacing.
key_takeaways: Constructing real-time, low-latency audio pipelines in Go using WebRTC and bi-directional gRPC.
Embedding ONNX runtimes inside Go for sub-8ms local CPU speech activity classification.
Eliminating GC pause spikes during continuous PCM audio streaming using sync.Pool and ring buffers.
Designing state machines for preemption and verbal barge-in ('CROW') in conversational developer agents.

timed_outline.topics: Why cloud voice proxies fail developers, the 110ms conversational threshold

timed_outline.section_title: WebRTC & PCM Audio Pipeline Architecture in Go
timed_outline.topics: Handling live RTP audio streams, jitter buffers, local acoustic echo cancellation

timed_outline.section_title: Local ONNX Silero VAD CPU Inference
timed_outline.topics: Integrating ONNX runtimes via CGO/purego, 30ms frame classification under 8ms

timed_outline.section_title: Zero-Allocation Go: Taming the GC with sync.Pool
timed_outline.topics: Preventing memory churn during 48kHz audio ingestion, GC pacing optimization
Sub-38ms agent preemption demo, architecture wrap-up, and community Q&A
